q: What are Canada's three airspace regions?
a: Southern Control Area, Northern Control Area, and Arctic Control Area (SCA, NCA, ACA).

src.quote: The United States is divided into 22 Area Control Centers (ACCs). Canada is divided into three airspace regions: the Southern Control Area (SCA), Northern Control Area (NCA), and Arctic Control Area (ACA).
src.note: Ch 19 covers North America (US and Canada). The Canadian Domestic Airspace (CDA) is separately split into the Southern Domestic Airspace (SDA) and Northern Domestic Airspace (NDA).

q: Under FOM 125.3, what decompression procedure applies to an A330 over the Canadian Rockies?
a: The polygon procedures in FOM 11.2.9.1; initial descent altitude is always 17,000 ft or FL170.

src.quote: (737/A330) Initial descent altitude is always 17,000 ft or FL170.
src.note: Rev 125.1 removed the Decompression Procedure for the Canadian Rockies Mountain Range Region from 19.3 - Navigation; Rev 125.3 renumbered the polygon procedures to 11.2.9.1. The old 18,000 ft Rockies floor is no longer published anywhere in the FOM.

q: What is the takeoff/landing airspeed restriction in Canada near a controlled airport?
a: 200 kt, or minimum safe/clean speed if faster, below 3000 ft AFL within 10 miles, unless ATC assigns higher.

src.quote: Canada restricts speed to 200 kts or minimum safe speed (i.e., clean maneuver), whichever is faster, below 3000 AFL within 10 miles of a controlled airport
src.note: Note the AFL (above field level) reference and the 10-mile radius, distinct from the US below-10,000 ft/250 kt convention.

q: What is the Juneau Taku wind hazard?
a: Terrain-induced Gastineau Channel winds gusting 72 mph or more, causing windshear, rotors, and turbulence; JAWS alerts for them.

src.quote: Very strong wind gusts (72 mph or greater) can occur during these Taku wind events.
src.note: See JNU 10-7 JAWS. This is a North America weather-hazard item alongside Anchorage Turnagain Arm turbulence and the LA Santa Ana rotor.

q: On NOPAC routes between FL340 and FL400, what performance capabilities are required?
a: RCP240, RSP180, RNP4; separation 23 nm. FL180-330 or FL410 and above: 50 nm, RNP10.

src.quote: between FL340-FL400, the lateral route separation is 23 nm and requires aircraft to be capable of Required Communications Performance 240 (RCP240), Required Surveillance Performance 180 (RSP180), and Required Navigation Performance 4 (RNP4)
src.note: The 737/787/A321/A330 are RCP240, RSP180, and RNP4 capable unless an MEL reduces capability.

q: Within the Oakland Oceanic FIR, at what altitude do you set standard 29.92?
a: At or above 5500 ft MSL; the Hawaiian Islands domestic area uses QNE at FL180 and above, QNH below.

src.ref: FOM 20.7.1 - Altimeter Setting - Oakland Oceanic FIR/Hawaii
src.quote: at FL180 and above, to standard altimeter setting 29.92 (QNE).
src.note: The Oakland FIR 5500 ft MSL transition to QNE is a lower crossover than the standard FL180, a common trap for Pacific/Hawaii altimetry questions.

q: In the Pacific theater, what cruise Mach change must be reported to ARINC?
a: Any change of 0.02 or greater from the previously reported value; Mach is first reported at FIR entry.

src.ref: FOM 20.2.2 - Oceanic Cruise Mach - Reporting Requirement
src.quote: All subsequent changes of cruise Mach of 0.02 or greater from any previously reported value must be communicated to ARINC.
src.note: FIR-entry Mach can be reported at check-in with ARINC (e.g., San Francisco Radio), via ADS-C, or free-text CPDLC. The 0.02 threshold mirrors the NAT/Atlantic Mach technique.

q: In Pacific oceanic airspace with a total loss of communications, what transponder sequence is used?
a: 7700 for one minute, then 7600 for 15 minutes or the remainder of the flight, whichever first; repeat as practicable.

src.ref: FOM 20.4.4 - Lost Communications in Oceanic Airspace
src.quote: adjust the transponder to Code 7700 for a period of 1 (one) minute. Then change to code 7600 and remain on 7600 for a period of 15 minutes or the remainder of the flight, whichever occurs first.
src.note: Replying on 7700 first increases probability of early detection of the radio failure. In IMC, maintain last assigned speed and flight level for 20 minutes after failing to report over a compulsory point, then follow the filed flight plan.

q: What are the maximum speed restrictions for operations in Mexico's National airspace?
a: 250 KIAS at or below 10,000 ft; 200 KIAS within 10 nm of any airport below 3000 ft AGL.

src.quote: Maximum Speed 200 KIAS within 10 nm of any airport below 3000 ft AGL above airport elevation.
src.note: Certain Mexican airports restrict airspeed in National airspace at or below 18,000 ft, so check the applicable STARs.

q: In the Central America portion of the Caribbean theater, what are the transition level and transition altitude?
a: Transition Level is FL200 and Transition Altitude is 19,000 ft MSL, unless charted otherwise.

src.quote: Transition Level is FL200 and Transition Altitude is 19,000 ft MSL unless charted otherwise.
src.note: Central America scheduled operations are Belize, Costa Rica, and Guatemala. 'Climb via'/'descend via' are NOT used in Central America (21.3.4.3).

q: In Mexico, what is the rule regarding visual approaches relative to distance from the airport?
a: Visual approaches are not permitted outside 10 nm; specifically request a 'visual descent' or 'visual approach'.

src.ref: FOM 21.3.3.5 - Mexico Phraseology for Climbs and Descents
src.quote: Mexico prohibits visual approaches outside of 10 nm.
src.note: A visual descent (remain on arrival routing, provide own terrain clearance) differs from a visual approach (routings/altitudes not restricted); the crew accepts responsibility for separation from traffic and terrain.

q: What flight levels define the North Atlantic High Level Airspace (NAT HLA)?
a: FL285 to FL420 inclusive, within Bodo, Gander, New York East, Reykjavik, Santa Maria, and Shanwick oceanic control areas.

src.quote: defined as the volume of airspace between flight levels 285 and 420 (inclusive)
src.note: Note NAT HLA spans FL285-FL420, which is wider than the FL290-FL410 RVSM/NAT DLM band. Source: NAT DOC 007, March 2025.

q: What are the NAT Organized Track System hours of validity at 30W?
a: Westbound 1130-1900 UTC; eastbound 0100-0800 UTC.

src.ref: FOM 22.3.1 - North Atlantic Organized Track System (OTS)
src.quote: Eastbound tracks, primarily used at night, are constructed by Gander Oceanic, while westbound tracks, used during the day, are constructed by Shanwick Oceanic.
src.note: OTS use is not mandatory; random routes are permitted. Times can be negotiated between Gander and Shanwick OACs, so check the NAT track message.

q: What are the RCL message timing intervals prior to the OEP for Gander, Shanwick, Santa Maria, and Bodo?
a: Gander 60-90 minutes; Shanwick 30-90 minutes; Santa Maria at least 40 minutes; Bodo at least 20 minutes.

src.quote: Gander: 60-90 minutes.
src.note: Except for Shanwick OCA, oceanic clearances are no longer issued in NAT OCAs; New York East does not require an RCL message at all. Shanwick still issues an oceanic clearance following the RCL.

q: How is the Northern Area of Magnetic Unreliability (AMU) defined?
a: Within 1000 nm of the Northern Magnetic Pole, excluding Alaska, plus Canadian Northern Domestic Airspace; all references are True North.

src.ref: FOM 22.2.3 - Northern Area of Magnetic Unreliability (AMU)
src.quote: navigation in the AMU relies on true headings rather than magnetic headings.
src.note: If ATC issues a heading in the AMU, confirm whether it is magnetic or true. In the AMU the Heading Reference switch is moved from NORM to TRUE, and HDG SEL must be reselected after the switch change (NAT HLA training, FCOM SP.10.1).

q: Under FOM 125.3, what decompression procedure applies to an A330 over the Greenland Mountain Range?
a: Polygon procedures in FOM 11.2.9.1; initial descent always to 17,000 ft or FL170; no charted No Ops Area transit.

src.quote: Dispatchers and pilots will not permit flights to proceed through any areas charted as “No Ops Area.”
src.note: Rev 125.1 removed the Decompression Procedure for Greenland Mountain Range Region from 22.5 - Weather. The old 15,000 ft Greenland floor is no longer published. Greenland overflight limits (22.11) point to the polygon procedures in 11.2.9.1.

q: How must European 8.33 kHz VHF frequencies be read back?
a: Exactly, with three decimal places: 132.015 MHz is 'WUN-TREE-TOO decimal ZE-RO-WUN-FIFE.'

src.quote: Europe utilizes 8.33 kHz channel spacing across much of its airspace
src.note: Capability is confirmed with 'CONFIRM EIGHT POINT THREE THREE' / 'AFFIRM EIGHT POINT THREE THREE' / 'NEGATIVE EIGHT POINT THREE THREE.'

q: What lateral navigation accuracy does European RNAV 5 (formerly B-RNAV) require?
a: Within 5 nm for at least 95% of enroute flight time; the A330 complies unless degraded by inoperative equipment.

src.quote: a lateral navigation accuracy of ±5 nm for at least 95% of the flight time.
src.note: For non-RNAV 5 compliant aircraft, notify ATC and Dispatch; Dispatch may obtain authorization to operate with the remaining nav equipment.

q: In the Republic of Korea, what buffer must crews observe around the DMZ?
a: Do not overfly the DMZ; a buffer zone extends 5 nm south of it.

src.quote: a buffer zone extends 5 nm south of the DMZ.
src.note: The Korea Office of Civil Aviation (KOCA) oversees all civil aviation activities; operations are under strict ATC control due to high traffic density and proximity to military-controlled zones.

q: What navigation approval must the A330 hold for a PACOTS track?
a: RNP10/RNAV10 or RNP4; where the track joins a NOPAC route, RCP240, RSP180, and RNP4 apply.

src.quote: An aircraft on a PACOTS track must be RNP10/RNAV10 or RNP4 approved. If the PACOTS track ends on a NOPAC route, the route requirements of RCP240, RSP180, and RNP4 apply.
src.note: Check-airman scenario. Related: the CEP (Central East Pacific, FOM 20.3.5) is the organized route system between Hawaii and California with seven charted ATS routes (R463, R464, R465, R576, R577, R578, R585) plus A331/A332 to the Pacific Northwest.

q: With one IRS failed at the gate, can the A330 dispatch into NAT HLA?
a: No. NAT HLA requires dual Inertial Reference Systems; no single-IRU relief exists for the A330.

src.ref: FOM 22.1.10, Required Equipment for NAT HLA Airspace
src.quote: • Dual Inertial Reference Systems (IRS) • Dual Long Range Navigation Systems (to include 2 MCDUs) • Dual Navigation Displays (ND) • One GPS Receiver • ADS-C • CPDLC • SATCOM data link • Two HF Radios or a single HF Radio and SATVOICE
src.note: Equipment failure after pushback but before entry that removes CPDLC and/or ADS-C: requests to operate in NAT DLM airspace are considered case by case; notify ATC and Dispatch as soon as possible.

q: How do you build a weather deviation offset in Pacific oceanic cruise?
a: Use the FMS Lateral Offset, not a route modification; request the deviation stating WEATHER DEVIATION REQUIRED for priority.

src.quote: Weather avoidance offsets must be accomplished utilizing the FMC/FMS Lateral Offset feature. Select a nm offset distance that will provide an adequate weather avoidance distance and request that track deviation from Oceanic Control; the clearance will generally be granted as “up to” the requested offset distance.
src.note: Contingency procedures for a deviation without a clearance are in the theater chapter and ICAO Doc 4444; brief them for the crossing.

q: Descending into Hawaii through the Oakland Oceanic FIR, at what altitude must the altimeter already be on 29.92?
a: At or above 5500 ft MSL, not FL180; the FL180 transition applies only in the Hawaiian Islands domestic area.

src.ref: FOM 20.7.1 - Altimeter Setting - Oakland Oceanic FIR/Hawaii
src.quote: Within all areas of the Oakland FIR, at or above 5500 ft MSL, the altimeter will be set to the standard 29.92 (QNE).
src.note: Check-airman scenario. Contrast with the Atlantic/Europe convention (FOM 22.1.7 / 23.10) where settings are given in hectopascals (hPa) and transition altitudes are charted while transition levels come from the ATIS or approach controller.

q: Where is the Oceanic Entry Point (OEP) defined in FOM Chapter 22?
a: FOM 22.2.2; 22.2.1 is 'Transition Areas' and 22.2.3 is the Northern Area of Magnetic Unreliability.

src.quote: Note that exceptions to common rules may exist. For example, a unique feature of the GOTA is that it has OEPs in the middle of the airspace which requires SLOP procedures halfway through the transition area. Also, eastbound flights through the GOTA are to send an RCL message to Gander Oceanic.
src.note: Chapter 22 renumbering is NEW in Rev 125: 22.2.1 Transition Areas, 22.2.2 OEP, 22.2.3 AMU, 22.2.4 West Atlantic.

q: What is the jumpseat rule into and out of London Heathrow?
a: Jumpseaters are not authorized into or out of LHR unless operationally required.

src.quote: Per local regulations, jumpseaters are not authorized into/out of LHR unless operationally required.
src.note: NEW section in Rev 125. LHR subsections renumbered under 23.18.1; 23.19 Italy is a new chapter.

q: Why can a SELCAL alert be misleading?
a: SELCAL codes are not unique; the call may be for another aircraft, so use proper phraseology and check callsigns.

src.quote: SELCAL codes are not unique. It is possible to receive a SELCAL notification that is intended for another aircraft. When responding to SELCAL notifications, crews should use proper radio phraseology and pay close attention to callsigns to avoid miscommunication.
src.note: New caution in Rev 125.

q: How do crewmembers entering Hawaii from the mainland complete the agriculture declaration?
a: Complete the digital Plant and Animals Declaration Form before arrival, accessed via the icon on the EFB.

src.quote: Hawaii requires all passengers and crewmembers that are entering Hawaii from the mainland to complete a digital “Plant and Animals Declaration Form” prior to arrival. The form can be accessed by crewmembers via the icon on their EFB.
src.note: Rev 125 moved the form to a digital EFB process. Departing Hawaii for the mainland, crewmembers process through a USDA station.

q: North of what latitude does A330 Inmarsat SATCOM become unreliable?
a: 72 degrees N; no coverage north of 80 degrees N, where Inmarsat CPDLC or SATVOICE is not an LRCS.

src.ref: FOM 19.4.1.3, SATCOM Service Limitations North of 72 North
src.quote: Due to satellite coverage limitations, flights operating with (787/A321/A330) Inmarsat equipment only may experience SATCOM unreliability north of 72°N. There is no Inmarsat satellite coverage north of 80°N. An Inmarsat CPDLC or SATVOICE system does not qualify as a Long-Range Communication System (LRCS) when operating north of 80°N.
src.note: Only the 737 Iridium SATVOICE is available north of 80 degrees N.

q: In the Atlantic theater, when must the crew perform a SELCAL check before entering each OCA?
a: Outside VHF coverage, before entering each OCA, on the designated HF frequencies.

src.quote: When operating outside of VHF coverage, prior to entering each individual OCA, the crew must perform a SELCAL check on the designated HF frequencies to establish and confirm voice communication.
src.note: Rev 125 qualified the requirement by VHF coverage. The logon goes to the controlling authority for the OCA, not the FIR.

q: What are crews not permitted to bring into Iceland?
a: Alcohol, tobacco products, and cash over $15,000.

src.quote: crews are not permitted to bring the following into Iceland: • Alcohol • Tobacco products • Cash over $15,000
src.note: New in Rev 125 with the Iceland section.

q: In Europe, can the A330 use the ground-based ATN data link network?
a: No. The A330's FANS 1/A(+) does not support ATN.

src.quote: The A330 has FANS 1/A (+) which does not support the ATN network.
src.note: Plan on FANS 1/A+ CPDLC service in Europe; ATN-only services are not available to the A330.
